items.match_in_review2: The Section 5 discussion attributing lower proprietary bias to "continuous monitoring and iterative refinement" is unsupported speculation — paper's discussion/interpretation overstates or downplays what the data actually shows.

items.text: The derivation of SOP orthogonality (Section 3.4) relies on an undefined term ("angular matrix"), making the disentanglement claim incomplete/insufficiently justified.
The one-shot VC result (50.46% WER) is better than baselines but not practically usable, yet framed as "effective" — overclaiming relative to absolute performance.

Trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and disentanglement. On clean speech reconstruction (Table 1), DeCodec achieves lower SDR than EnCodec and substantially worse Mel distance than DAC (0.89 vs. 0.65), suggesting that the decoupling mechanism may come at a non-trivial cost in acoustic quality. This trade-off is not thoroughly discussed.

High WER in one-shot voice conversion. Even with noise removal, the converted speech WER (50.46%) is very high, far beyond what is considered usable for speech conversion. The authors acknowledge voicing mismatch as a cause, but this severely limits the practical value of the VC application.

Heuristic theoretical justification. The proof using the mean value theorem relies on a linear approximation of the decoder and assumes the existence of ξ in a way that is not rigorous for a deep neural network. The argument is more intuitive than formal, which weakens the claimed theoretical guarantee.
items.match_in_review2: Questionable core assumption: the paper's core theoretical/methodological assumption (independence from demographics implies unbiasedness) is not rigorously justified and may not hold, undermining the validity of the proposed metric.

items.text: Reliance on clean speech for HuBERT supervision. The semantic guidance loss requires clean speech signals during training, limiting training data to mixtures where clean reference is available, which may constrain generalization to in-the-wild noisy data.
items.match_in_review2: Confounding due to image-based demographic inference: the method relies on the model's own recognition of attributes from images, an unaddressed limitation/confound in the experimental setup that may constrain validity of results.

items.text: Limited evaluation metrics for speech enhancement. Only DNSMOS non-intrusive metrics are reported. Adding PESQ or STOI would strengthen the speech enhancement comparison, especially since baseline models were originally evaluated on these metrics.

Single HuBERT layer (L9) used. The choice of which layer and model size is not ablated. The semantic guidance may be sensitive to this choice, and the robustness of the decomposition to different semantic targets is not explored.

items.text: The relabeling strategy of this paper is essentially equivalent to penalizing unsafe state-action pairs with a large negative reward. I think this idea is not novel. There is a paper with a similar idea, which also penalizes unsafe state-action pairs with a large negative reward (or a small reward).

The authors claim that the proposed method can enforce state-action-wise safety constraints. However, the method cannot guarantee that the learned policy will not visit unsafe state-action pairs, because the penalty is based on the estimated Q-function, which may not be accurate, especially at the beginning of training.

items.text: The PSR 'theoretical basis' is invoked but not operationalized — claims of guarantees from PSR theory are an overstatement not backed by design constraints.
The dynamics model is simple relative to the practical claims made (congestion factor doesn't capture real spatiotemporal traffic complexity).
Manual tuning of k and n is a practical limitation, understating the challenge of deployment in new settings without principled hyperparameter selection.
items.match_in_review2: The selective restoration policies in Table 3 are not explained — unclear how policies were chosen, limiting practical applicability/interpretability of the approach (Major #3).

items.text: Limited novelty relative to existing work: The core idea of using shortest-path-based subgraph extraction and local neighborhood features for state representation in graph-based RL is not fundamentally new. The paper does not adequately differentiate its contributions from existing graph sparsification or attention-based methods in the RL literature.
Theoretical grounding is overstated: The paper invokes PSR to claim theoretical sufficiency of the compressed features, but does not provide any formal proof or rigorous argument.

Baseline comparison is incomplete and potentially unfair: DFR is compared against an unrealistic straw-man 'All Dynamics' baseline, missing comparisons against more realistic baselines (local k-hop features, random subgraph sampling, GNN-based encoders, traditional feature selection).
items.match_in_review2: Unfair comparison on the MDB benchmark: baselines are trained only on primitive distortions while PRISM is trained on compound mixtures, giving PRISM an advantage; baselines should be retrained/fine-tuned on the same data for a fair comparison.

items.text: Limited analysis of computational overhead: The paper claims 'negligible additional computational overhead' but does not report the pre-training cost of the distance-based policy or the subgraph extraction time; only inference time is reported.

Parameter sensitivity is not fully resolved: The ablation study shows complex interactions between k and n, and the paper's recommendation for parameter selection is vague without a principled criterion.
items.match_in_review2: Limited analysis of prompt sensitivity: prompt variation sensitivity is mentioned as analyzed in the appendix, but the main text provides no quantification of how much performance varies with different phrasings.

items.text: The paper uses 'dynamics' and 'dynamic' in a potentially confusing way (footnote 1), though this is clarified.

items.text: The proposed method requires training a clustering codebook, which may be time-consuming and computationally expensive. The paper does not provide sufficient details on the computational resources required for this training, making it difficult to assess the practical feasibility of the approach. Furthermore, the convergence of the clustering codebook training is not discussed, which is crucial for the stability of the method.

The proposed method may not be suitable for real-time applications due to its computational complexity. The paper lacks a detailed analysis of the inference time complexity, particularly concerning the token permutation and global prior prompting modules. The computational overhead of these modules could be significant, especially for high-resolution images, making the method impractical for real-time scenarios.
